groups.high: For many US nonimmigrant visa categories, INA section 214(b) presumes immigrant intent until the applicant establishes eligibility for the temporary category. This is not INA section 214(a)(2), and some categories, including H-1B and L visas, have different intent rules. For a visitor visa, the officer considers the applicant's circumstances, purpose, travel plans, finances and ties outside the United States. Employment, study, family responsibilities, residence and community connections can support an intention to leave after a temporary visit. No universal checklist requires property ownership, a spouse or a particular amount of wealth, and no document guarantees approval. Explain the genuine purpose and duration of travel and how it will be funded; use accurate evidence and answer honestly. A 214(b) refusal concerns that application and is not itself a permanent ban. A new application generally requires a new form and fee; significant changes in circumstances may be relevant. A visa permits seeking admission, not a guaranteed period of stay; border authorities determine admission and authorised duration.
groups.mid: Many US temporary visa applicants must overcome a presumption of immigrant intent under INA section 214(b). That means showing they qualify for a temporary visit and will leave as required. Some visas, such as H-1B and L, have different intent rules. For a visitor visa, the officer checks your purpose, plans, funds and ties outside the US. A job, studies, family duties, a home and community links may support your case. There is no fixed rule that everyone must own property or have a spouse. No paper guarantees approval. Explain why you will travel, how long you plan to stay and how you will pay. Give true facts and honest answers. A refusal under 214(b) applies to that application. It is not by itself a permanent ban. A fresh application normally needs a new form and fee. Important changes in your situation may matter. A visa lets you ask to enter; it does not guarantee entry or the length of stay. Border officials decide those.
groups.low: Many US temporary visas need proof that the trip is temporary. The rule is INA section 214(b), not section 214(a)(2). Some visas, such as H-1B and L, have different rules. For a visitor visa, say why you want to go. Say how long you will stay and how you will pay. The officer looks at your plans and life outside the US. A job, school, family duties, home or local ties may help show you will leave. You do not always need to own a house or have a spouse. No paper can promise approval. Tell the truth and use real evidence. A 214(b) refusal is for that application. It is not by itself a permanent ban. To apply again, you usually need a new form and fee. A big change in your situation may matter. A visa lets you ask to enter. It does not promise entry or a fixed stay. Border staff make that choice.
groups.source_review: Checked State Department 214(b) intent, individual ties and reapplication guidance.
groups.notes: Corrected statute, categorical home-ties failure and invented mandatory property/family criteria; clarified visa versus admission.

groups.high: Passport-validity requirements depend on the destination, nationality, travel document and route. For many US visitors, a passport must be valid for six months beyond the intended stay, but Six-Month Club agreements waive that additional period for eligible nationalities. In those cases the passport generally must remain valid for the intended stay. Do not assume Canada, the United Kingdom or the Schengen Area all apply the same US rule. For ordinary Schengen short visits, a common requirement is validity for at least three months after intended departure and issuance within the preceding ten years, subject to applicable rules and exceptions. Passport expiry, visa validity and authorised stay are separate dates. Check destination and transit authorities and the airline before booking, including document type and nationality-specific exemptions. Renew early if necessary. A failure can prevent boarding or admission, but a short passport validity does not automatically impose a future travel ban. Calculate any required buffer from the date specified by that country's rule, not automatically from entry.
groups.mid: Passport rules vary by country and the passport you hold. For many US visitors, the passport must last six months past the planned stay. The Six-Month Club removes that extra time for some passport holders. Their passports usually just need to last for the stay. Do not assume Canada, the UK and Schengen all use the US rule. For many short Schengen visits, the passport must last three months past the planned exit. It should have been issued in the last ten years. Check the exact rule and any exceptions. Passport expiry, visa expiry and the last day you may stay are different dates. Check all countries on the route and the airline before booking. Say which passport and type of document you hold. Renew early if needed. A short-validity passport may stop you boarding or entering. It does not mean an automatic future travel ban. Count months from the date the real rule uses. It may not be the entry date.
groups.low: Check passport rules for each country on your route. Rules depend on your passport and document type. Many US visitors need six months left after their planned stay. Some passport holders are in the Six-Month Club. For them, the passport usually just needs to cover the stay. Canada, the UK and Schengen do not all use the US rule. For many short Schengen trips, the passport needs three months left after you leave. It should also have been issued in the last ten years. Check for exceptions. Passport expiry is one date. Visa expiry is another. Neither alone says how long you may stay. Ask each country's border staff before you book. Ask your airline too. Renew early if needed. An early expiry may stop you boarding or entering. It does not mean an automatic future ban. Count months from the date the rule says. It may not be when you enter.
groups.source_review: Checked CBP Six-Month Club exception and European Commission Schengen document guidance.
groups.notes: Corrected universal six-month claim, entry/departure inconsistency and categorical ban/deportation consequences.

groups.high: B-1 business and B-2 visitor status do not generally authorise local employment or ordinary productive work in the United States. Permitted B-1 activities can include consultations, conferences and contract negotiations; B-2 generally covers tourism, visiting and certain other temporary purposes. Working remotely for a foreign payer is not automatically lawful simply because the pay comes from abroad. However, the rule is not an absolute ban on every US-source payment. Reimbursement of reasonable incidental travel expenses and narrowly defined academic honoraria may be permitted under specific conditions. The academic exception involves qualifying institutions, activities lasting no more than nine days at one institution and payments or expenses from no more than five institutions in the previous six months, among other conditions. It is not general work permission. Particular visitor arrangements have additional rules. Confirm the proposed duties and payment structure with official guidance or qualified immigration counsel before acting. Unauthorised work can affect status and future immigration eligibility, but removal or a permanent ban is not automatic in every case.
groups.mid: B-1 and B-2 visitor status usually do not let you take a job in the US. They do not allow ordinary work. B-1 can cover meetings, conferences and contract talks. B-2 generally covers tourism and visits. Being paid abroad does not automatically make remote work lawful. Not all US payments are banned. Some cases allow reasonable travel costs. A narrow rule allows some academic honoraria. These are payments for certain academic tasks, such as a guest lecture. It has strict conditions. The institution must qualify. The activity must be no more than nine days at one institution. Pay or expenses must not come from more than five institutions in the last six months. Other rules apply too. It does not allow a normal job. Some visitor arrangements have separate rules. Check the duties and pay in official guidance first. Or ask a qualified immigration lawyer. Work without permission can harm status and future applications. It does not mean everyone must be removed or banned for life.
groups.low: A B-1 or B-2 visitor usually cannot take a US job. Ordinary work is not allowed. B-1 can cover meetings, conferences and contract talks. B-2 is usually for visits or tourism. Pay from abroad does not make remote work legal by itself. But some US payments may be allowed. These can include reasonable travel costs in a permitted visit. A narrow rule allows some academic honoraria. This means pay for tasks such as a guest lecture. The host institution must meet the rules. It must last no more than nine days at one institution. You must not take such pay or costs from more than five institutions in six months. Other rules apply too. This does not allow a normal job. Some visitor cases have their own rules. Check the duties and pay before you start. Use official guidance or ask a qualified lawyer who handles visas. Work without permission can harm your status and later visa requests. It does not mean you must be sent out or banned for life in all cases.
groups.source_review: Checked State visitor guidance and FAM expense/honorarium exceptions.
groups.notes: Corrected absolute any-US-payment ban, foreign-pay automatic exclusion and automatic permanent sanctions.

groups.high: Overstaying an authorised US admission is not the same as entering unlawfully. Authorised stay, visa expiry and unlawful presence are related but distinct concepts. INA section 212(a)(9)(B) provides a three-year inadmissibility bar in qualifying circumstances following more than 180 days but less than one year of unlawful presence and departure. One year or more can trigger a ten-year bar following departure or removal. The calculation is not simply every day after a visa sticker expires, and the three-year provision has specific departure and proceedings conditions. Periods before age 18 and certain other statutory exceptions may not count. Remaining in the US does not by itself activate these departure-triggered bars, although other status and removal consequences may arise. Waivers and other relief depend on the category and facts. Certain immigrant waivers require extreme hardship to a qualifying US-citizen or lawful-permanent-resident spouse or parent, not simply any child. Do not leave, remain or file a waiver based only on a general summary; obtain case-specific advice from a qualified immigration professional.
groups.mid: Overstaying in the US is not the same as entering illegally. The visa expiry date is not always the date your stay ends. Check your admission record and status. The rule is INA section 212(a)(9)(B). More than 180 days but less than one year of unlawful presence can lead to a three-year bar. It applies after departure in qualifying cases. One year or more can lead to a ten-year bar. This can follow departure or removal. Exactly 180 days is not the same as more than 180. The rules also have conditions about departure and proceedings. Some time may not count. This includes time before age 18 and other legal exceptions. These bars do not start just because a person remains in the US, though other consequences can apply. Waivers depend on the facts and visa type. Some immigrant waivers require extreme hardship to a qualifying relative. That can mean a US-citizen or permanent-resident spouse or parent, not simply any child. Get qualified case-specific advice before deciding to leave, stay or apply for relief.
groups.low: An overstay is not the same as an illegal entry. Your visa's expiry date may not be the last day you can stay. Check your admission record and status. The rule here is INA section 212(a)(9)(B). More than 180 days but less than one year of unlawful presence may cause a three-year bar. It applies after leaving in some cases. One year or more may cause a ten-year bar. It applies after leaving or removal. Exactly 180 days is not more than 180 days. Rules cover how you leave and whether legal proceedings began. Some time does not count. Time before age 18 and other legal exceptions may be left out. These bars do not start just because you stay in the US. Other harms to your status may still apply. Some waivers need extreme hardship to a spouse or parent who is a US citizen or permanent resident. Having a child alone may not meet the rule. Get expert legal advice first. Do not decide to leave, stay or seek a waiver from this guide alone.
groups.source_review: Reviewed federal statutory text and official guidance identity; USCIS direct page retrieval failed. Not a personalised calculation.
groups.notes: Corrected illegal-entry equivalence, exactly180 threshold, departure trigger, omitted10-year bar, child-hardship waiver and depart-first-only advice.

groups.high: For ordinary short stays covered by the Schengen rules, third-country nationals may spend no more than 90 days in any rolling 180-day period. On every day of stay, count that day and the preceding 179 days, combining relevant stays across the Schengen Area. Entry and exit days both count. Leaving one Schengen country for another does not restart the allowance, and briefly leaving the area does not reset it. Earlier days cease to count as they fall outside the moving window. A continuous absence of 90 days generally permits a fresh stay of up to 90 days, subject to all other entry and visa conditions. A visa can authorise fewer days or expire sooner than the general allowance. Residence permits, long-stay visas, free-movement rights and certain agreements require separate analysis; permission in one country does not universally exempt travel elsewhere. Use the European Commission calculator and official advice for the itinerary. Overstaying can lead to national penalties, removal or entry restrictions; there is no single automatic fine or ban for every case.
groups.mid: For normal short Schengen visits, the limit is 90 days in any rolling 180 days. On each day, count that day plus the previous 179 days. Add all relevant visits across the Schengen Area. Both the entry and exit day count. Moving from one Schengen country to another does not reset the clock. A short trip outside the area does not reset it either. Old days stop counting when they fall outside the window. After 90 days away in a row, a fresh stay of up to 90 days is usually possible. Other entry rules must still be met. A visa may allow fewer days or end sooner. Other rules may apply to long-stay visas and residence permits. Free-movement rights and special agreements also need separate checks. A permit for one country does not remove all limits on visiting others. Use the European Commission's calculator and check your exact route. An overstay may lead to fines, removal or limits on return under national law. There is no one automatic penalty for every case.
groups.low: Many Schengen short visits use a 90-in-180-day rule. Each day, count that day and the 179 days before it. Add the days from all relevant Schengen trips. You must stay at 90 days or less. Entry and exit days count too. Moving to another Schengen country does not start a new count. A quick trip outside does not reset it. Old days leave the count as time moves on. After 90 days away in a row, a new stay of up to 90 days is generally possible if other rules are met. Your visa may allow less time or expire sooner. A residence permit or long-stay visa needs a separate check. So do free-movement rights and special agreements. One country's permit does not remove every rule for trips to others. Use the European Commission calculator and check the route. An overstay can cause fines, removal or limits on return. The penalty depends on national law and the case.
groups.source_review: Checked European Commission rolling-window guidance and calculator manual.
groups.notes: Corrected nonsensical January/July example, false year-away no-reentry claim, broad permit exemptions and fixed-ban claims.

groups.high: A machine-readable passport is not necessarily an electronic passport. A conventional machine-readable travel document can use the printed machine-readable zone without a chip. An ePassport adds a contactless integrated circuit, identified by the ePassport symbol, storing specified biographical and biometric data and a digital security object under ICAO Doc 9303. A facial image is the primary interoperable biometric; fingerprints or iris data may be optional and subject to national rules. ISO/IEC standards and the document's edition govern technical formats, so ISO/IEC 19794-2 should not be described as the facial-image standard: it concerns fingerprint minutiae, while facial-image formats have separate specifications. Digital-signature validation checks authenticity and integrity of chip data. It is distinct from comparing the live traveller with the facial image and does not guarantee perfect identity matching. ICAO's Public Key Directory supports exchange of certificate information needed for validation, not passport holders' personal data. Check the destination's document requirements, since an electronically chipped passport may be required for particular travel programmes even though not all machine-readable documents are electronic.
groups.mid: Not all machine-readable passports have chips. A printed machine-readable zone can be scanned on its own. An ePassport adds a contactless chip and usually shows an ePassport symbol. ICAO Doc 9303 sets out what the chip stores. It holds biographical and biometric data. It also holds a digital security object. The facial image is the main biometric for use across systems. Fingerprints or iris data may be optional under national rules. Standards and the document edition set the data formats. ISO/IEC 19794-2 is for fingerprint minutiae. It is not the facial-image standard. The face has separate specifications. A digital-signature check tests chip data. It shows whether the data is authentic and unchanged. Comparing a live face to the image is a separate check. It cannot promise a perfect match. ICAO's Public Key Directory shares certificate information for these checks. It does not share the holder's personal data. Check destination and travel-programme rules. Some trips require an ePassport. Not all machine-readable documents have a chip.
groups.low: A machine-readable passport may have no electronic chip. The printed machine-readable zone can be scanned on its own. An ePassport adds a contactless chip. It usually shows the ePassport symbol. ICAO Doc 9303 sets out the data on it. This includes biographical data, biometric data and a digital security object. The face image is the main biometric used across systems. Fingerprints or iris data may be optional. It depends on national rules. The standards and document edition set the formats. ISO/IEC 19794-2 is for fingerprint minutiae. It is not for face images. Face images have their own specifications. A digital-signature check tests chip data. It shows whether it is authentic and unchanged. Comparing the traveller's face with that image is another check. These checks do not promise a perfect match. The ICAO Public Key Directory shares certificate information. This is used for validation. It does not share passport holders' personal data. Check the destination and travel programme. Some need an ePassport. Not every machine-readable document contains a chip.
groups.source_review: Checked ICAO ePassport distinction, signatures, facial biometric and PKD role; technical format correction qualified by editions.
groups.notes: Corrected all-MRTD-must-have-chip claim, 19794-2 facial attribution and perfect matching guarantees. Original Low FK higher than Mid; overlap permits only a narrow Mid>Low range.

groups.high: A destination or transit itinerary may require evidence of yellow-fever vaccination under the International Health Regulations (2005). The International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis becomes valid 10 days after primary vaccination and remains valid for the vaccinated person's lifetime under the amended Annex 7. It may be completed at vaccination; it is not prohibited from being issued during the ten-day period. Lifetime validity includes certificates issued before the amendment took effect on 11 July 2016; an old ten-year expiry entry does not by itself require a booster for certificate validity. Use an appropriately designated vaccination centre and ensure the certificate is properly completed, signed and stamped. WHO approves relevant vaccines, but national authorities designate centres and clinicians. Entry requirements depend on country, age, origin and transit history, not simply whether travel is to Africa or South America. A certificate's lifetime validity does not determine whether vaccination is medically appropriate for an individual. Seek travel-health advice about contraindications, precautions and possible medical waivers, whose acceptance is not guaranteed. Check official requirements before travel.
groups.mid: Some destinations or transit routes require proof of yellow-fever vaccination. This is under the International Health Regulations (2005). The document is the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis. It becomes valid 10 days after the first vaccination. Under amended Annex 7, it remains valid for the person's lifetime. The certificate can be completed at the vaccination visit. There is no need to wait ten days to issue it. Lifetime validity also applies to older certificates. This includes those showing a ten-year expiry. The change took effect on 11 July 2016. That old entry alone does not require a booster. Use a nationally designated vaccination centre. Check the signature, stamp and recorded details. WHO approves relevant vaccines. National authorities designate centres and clinicians. Rules depend on destination, age, origin and transit history. They do not depend just on the continent. Lifetime certificate validity does not mean the vaccine is suitable for everyone. Ask a travel-health professional about risks and contraindications. Ask about possible medical waivers too. A country may not accept a waiver. Check official rules before travel.
groups.low: Some countries or transit routes ask for proof of a yellow-fever vaccine. The rule comes from the International Health Regulations (2005). The document is the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis. It is valid 10 days after the first vaccine. Under amended Annex 7, it then lasts for life. The centre can fill it in when you get the vaccine. It does not have to wait ten days to issue it. The lifetime rule began on 11 July 2016. It covers older certificates too. A printed ten-year expiry does not by itself mean you need a booster. Go to a nationally designated vaccine centre. Check the details, signature and stamp. WHO approves the vaccines. National authorities choose centres and clinicians. Rules depend on the country and your age. They also depend on where you came from and transit stops. A lifetime certificate does not mean the vaccine is safe for every person. Ask a travel-health expert about risks and any medical waiver. A waiver may not be accepted. Check official rules before you travel.
groups.source_review: Checked WHO Annex7 lifetime amendment, ten-day onset and prior-certificate treatment.
groups.notes: Corrected cannot-issue-before10days and WHO-authorised-clinician claims; added entry-specific requirements and clinical exceptions.

groups.high: The Hague Convention of 5 October 1961 Abolishing the Requirement of Legalisation for Foreign Public Documents replaces diplomatic or consular legalisation with an Apostille when the Convention applies between the relevant states. A designated Competent Authority in the place of origin issues the certificate. It verifies the signature, the capacity of the signer and, where appropriate, the seal or stamp; it does not certify the truth of the document's contents or guarantee its substantive legal effect abroad. Public documents can include court documents, administrative records, notarial acts and official certificates on private documents. Diplomatic or consular documents and certain administrative documents directly concerning commercial or customs operations are excluded. Check that the Convention is in force between the states, including any objections and territorial extensions, rather than relying on an outdated fixed country count. Translation and local admissibility requirements may remain. Electronic Apostilles can be used where properly issued; authenticity can be checked through the relevant authority or register. HCCH itself does not issue Apostilles. A valid Apostille removes the specified authentication chain, not every possible scrutiny of the underlying document.
groups.mid: The Hague Apostille Convention dates from 5 October 1961. It simplifies authentication of foreign public documents. It must apply between the two states. Then one Apostille replaces diplomatic or consular legalisation. A designated Competent Authority issues it. This is in the place where the document originates. The Apostille confirms the signature and the signer's official capacity. It also confirms any relevant seal or stamp. It does not prove the contents are true. It does not guarantee legal effect abroad. Public documents can include court and administrative records. Notarial acts and official certificates on private documents can qualify too. Diplomatic or consular documents and certain commercial or customs administrative documents are excluded. Check the current Convention relationship between the states. Objections or territorial rules may matter. Do not rely on a fixed number such as 125 countries. Translation and local acceptance rules can still apply. Properly issued electronic Apostilles may be used. Check them through the competent authority or register. HCCH does not issue them. An Apostille replaces authentication steps. Other checks on the underlying document may remain.
groups.low: The Hague Apostille Convention dates from 5 October 1961. It can replace a long process of legalisation for a foreign public document. One Apostille takes its place. It must apply between the two states. A designated Competent Authority issues it. This is where the document comes from. It confirms the signature and the signer's official role. It also confirms any relevant seal or stamp. It does not prove that the contents are true. It does not guarantee full legal effect abroad. Court records and administrative records can qualify. So can notarial acts and official certificates on private documents. Diplomatic or consular documents are excluded. Certain administrative documents are excluded too. These directly concern commercial or customs operations. Check the current rules between both states. Check objections and territorial limits too. Do not rely on an old count of 125 countries. You may still need a translation. Other local rules may apply. A valid e-Apostille can also be used. Check it through the proper authority or register. HCCH itself does not issue Apostilles. Other checks on the document may still be allowed.
groups.source_review: Checked treaty scope, Competent Authorities and limited effect of certification; current count not asserted.
groups.notes: Corrected content/legal-validity guarantee, blanket translations coverage, outdated125 count and missing exclusions.

groups.high: Transit-visa requirements must be checked for the exact nationality, travel document, itinerary and airport. Some travellers need an airport-transit visa even when remaining airside; others qualify for an exemption based on nationality, residence permits, visas or onward travel. Passing immigration to collect baggage, change airports, use a landside hotel or meet a connection can require ordinary entry permission rather than an airside-transit visa. Terminal changes do not always require entry, so verify the actual route and airport arrangements. There is no universal visa-free 24–72-hour transit allowance. Time limits, confirmed tickets, destination documents and permitted activities vary. Check the transit government's official guidance and the airline's documentation check, such as IATA Timatic or Travel Centre, before buying a complex itinerary. Recheck after schedule or route changes and shortly before departure. An airline's database assists compliance but does not replace the law or guarantee border admission. Missing documents can cause denied boarding, refused entry and substantial travel costs.
groups.mid: Check transit rules for your exact passport, nationality, route and airport. Some people need an airport-transit visa even if they stay airside. Others may be exempt because of their nationality, residence permit, other visas or onward trip. If you must pass immigration to collect bags, change airports or use a landside hotel, you may need normal entry permission. An airside-transit visa may not cover that. A terminal change does not always mean crossing immigration, so check the actual airport route. There is no worldwide 24–72-hour visa-free transit rule. Time limits, onward tickets, destination papers and allowed activities differ. Check the transit government's official advice and the airline, which may use IATA Timatic or Travel Centre. Do this before buying a difficult connection. Recheck if the route or schedule changes and before departure. The airline's database helps with checks, but is not the law or a promise of entry. Missing papers may cause denied boarding, refused entry and extra costs.
groups.low: Transit rules depend on your passport and nationality. Your route and airport matter too. Some people need an airport-transit visa even while staying airside. Others may be exempt. This can depend on nationality, a residence permit, a visa or onward travel. Check before you book. You may need to pass immigration to collect bags or change airports. A landside hotel may need this too. In those cases, check normal entry permission. An airside visa may not be enough. Changing terminals does not always mean passing immigration. Ask about your exact connection. There is no global rule allowing 24–72 hours without a transit visa. Time limits, tickets, destination papers and allowed activities differ. Use the transit government's official advice and check with the airline. It may use IATA Timatic or Travel Centre. Recheck if flights or routes change. Check again before departure. A database helps with travel checks. It is not the law. It cannot promise entry. Missing papers can stop you boarding or entering. This may cost you money.
groups.source_review: Checked IATA personalised passport/visa/transit requirement function; no destination-specific eligibility claimed without itinerary.
groups.notes: Qualified visa-free interval and automatic terminal-change entry assumptions; airline database not law.

groups.high: US immigrant-visa police-certificate requirements are not limited to twelve-month stays. For applicants aged 16 or older, State Department guidance generally requires certificates from the country of nationality after more than six months' residence at any time, and the current residence country if different after more than six months. A former foreign residence of twelve months or more also requires a certificate when the applicant was at least 16 while living there. Arrests can require a certificate regardless of age or length of residence. US police certificates are not required for present or former US residents. Check the country-specific Reciprocity and Civil Documents guidance for availability, issuing authority and procedures. Certificates generally expire after two years, except for a former residence country not revisited since issue. Follow translation and interview instructions; do not assume every certificate needs an Apostille. If a required document is unavailable, follow the official explanation procedure rather than fabricating a substitute. Missing required records can delay the case; the consular officer determines what is needed before issuance.
groups.mid: For a US immigrant visa, police certificates are not only for stays of twelve months. If you are 16 or older, check your country of nationality. More than six months there at any time generally means you need a certificate. Is your current country of residence different? You need one there too after more than six months. For another country where you used to live, the rule is different. It is twelve months or more when you were at least 16. An arrest can require a certificate at any age. The length of stay does not matter. Current and former US residents do not need US police certificates. Use the State Department's Reciprocity and Civil Documents page. These explain where and how to apply in each country. Certificates generally expire after two years. For a former country, it can remain valid if you have not returned since issue. Follow the rules for translations and the interview. An Apostille is not always needed. If a required record is not available, explain why through the official process. Missing records can delay the case. The consular officer decides what is required.
groups.low: Police certificates for a US immigrant visa have several rules. If you are 16 or older, check your country of nationality. You generally need one after more than six months there at any time. Is your current country different? More than six months there also needs one. For another country where you used to live, the rule is different. It is twelve months or more when you were at least 16. If arrested, you may need a certificate at any age. The length of stay does not matter. You do not need US police certificates for present or past US residence. Check the State Department's Reciprocity and Civil Documents page for each country. It says if records are available. It tells you how to get them. Certificates generally expire after two years. For a former country, it can stay valid if you have not returned since issue. Follow translation and interview instructions. An Apostille is not always needed. If a record is not available, explain why through the official process. Missing papers may delay the case. The consular officer decides what must be provided.
groups.source_review: Checked State Department's full police-certificate table, arrest/US exceptions and expiry.
groups.notes: Corrected blanket12-month/post16 rule, missing6-month nationality/current-residence rules, arrest exception and unnecessary Apostille assumption.
